extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in NLP, IR, and misinformation detection (especially medical/health domains)
extracted.subtask_description: Survey-level taxonomy and evaluation criteria for computational methods to detect and validate health/medical misinformation on social media, covering KB-based, content-based, propagation-based, and graph-based approaches and their features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge Base Claim Validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert a textual claim to a triple (subject, predicate, object) and check the validity of the fact against a knowledge graph (KG); must account for the KG's incompleteness (Open World Assumption).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three approaches to handle incomplete KBs: (a) complement KB with external web resources (highly error-prone — e.g., 83.51% of fact-triples extracted from Wikipedia by a BERT RE approach were false), (b) embedding-based and path-based methods that use graph embeddings or path properties to verify facts (can verify entity links not present in KG), and (c) rule-based approaches using rule-mining (more interpretable and can verify facts embeddings struggle with). Embedding and rule-based approaches can be complementary and yield better performance when combined. Beware that missing facts in KG do not imply false claims due to Open World Assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-specific Knowledge Bases / Knowledge Graph Selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Select and use appropriate medical or domain-specific KGs/KBs (e.g., UMLS, SciClaim KG, KnowLife, COVID-specific graphs, DrugBank, disease ontologies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use KGs for normalization, candidate selection, and training embeddings (e.g., UMLS for normalization and cui2vec training). Note that KG quality varies (DBpedia v3.6 ~80% correct); verify source reliability and consider combining multiple KBs. KG schema choices (RDF/OWL) and inclusion of fine-grained attributes (e.g., SciClaim's causal/comparative labels) affect verification granularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge Embedding Models for KG-based Verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Use knowledge graph embedding/modeling methods (e.g., TransE, TransD, TransMS, TuckER) to create representations for link prediction and fact verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embedding approaches statistically infer plausibility of unlinked entity pairs and can extend verifiable triples beyond rule-based coverage; they have been applied to COVID-19 misinformation detection as graph link prediction. Combine with path-based or rule methods when interpretability or coverage of logical constraints is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text Representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert unstructured documents to vector representations: BoW, TF-IDF, n-grams, non-contextual embeddings, contextual embeddings, and knowledge embeddings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effectiveness of word/text embeddings affects downstream classifier performance. Non-contextual embeddings (word2vec, GloVe, FastText) give single global vectors per word; contextual embeddings (BERT and derivatives) assign context-dependent vectors and generally perform better in fake-news tasks. Choose representation based on task data size and domain; pre-trained representations reduce data collection costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-trained Language Models and Domain Fine-tuning
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage pre-trained transformer-based models (BERT, BART, RoBERTa, distilBERT, XLNet, etc.) and domain-specific variants (BioBERT, Med-BERT, SCIBERT, BioGPT, BERTweet, COVID-Twitter-BERT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fine-tuning on task-specific or domain-specific corpora (e.g., biomedical articles, EHRs, Twitter COVID tweets) substantially improves performance for medical fake-news tasks. Combining multiple pre-trained models (e.g., BERT + BERTweet + COVID-Twitter-BERT) can outperform single models because each captures complementary aspects (general English, tweet structure, domain terminology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic Features
rubrics_metrics.description: Morphological, syntactic, and grammatical features such as POS tags, noun phrases, POS n-grams, uncertainty constructs (possibility adverbs, conditional particles), certainty constructs, demonstratives, modal words, questions, superlatives, and passive voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features capture structural differences between fake and true news; headline size is a key element (headline length matters). Some findings: passive voice may correlate with trustworthy sources; POS n-grams did not always improve over TF-IDF baselines in certain studies. Use linguistic features alongside other feature types rather than standalone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional / Sentiment Features
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentiment polarity (positive/negative/neutral) and emotion detection (fear, anxiety, depression, anger, happiness, etc.) derived from text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fake news often provokes fear/anxiety; high negativity or depression correlates with subjectivity. Use established lexicons and tools (NRC, MPQA, ANEW, SentiWordNet, WordNet-Affect, text2emotion, TextBlob). Polarity can indicate bias and questionable credibility; include sentiment features as part of multi-feature classifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entity-based Features / Named Entity Recognition (NER)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect named entities (Person, Location, Organization, Event, Product, Dates, medical entities like diseases/drugs) and quantify entity-related signals (fraction of medical terms, named-entity patterns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biomedical NER models (e.g., MedMentions) improve detection in medical domains. Use entity counts and sequences (NER+POS) as classifier features. Additional signals: fraction of commercial terms (higher counts → lower credibility), number of direct quotes (unreliable outlets use fewer quotations), and number of hyperlinks (credible articles have on average ~1.6 more hyperlinks). Hashtags can help in early-stage detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific Content Signals: Headline Length, Quotes, Hyperlinks
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface-level content indicators: headline length, number of direct quotes, number of hyperlinks present in an article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headline size is a distinguishing feature between fake and true news. Reliable sources tend to include more direct quotations and more hyperlinks; unreliable outlets use fewer quotations. Quantify these counts as features in classifiers (e.g., average hyperlinks difference observed in studies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic Features
rubrics_metrics.description: Style-related attributes: informational density, complexity (chars/words ratio), non-immediacy (disassociative framing), lexical diversity, uncertainty/hedging, informality (emoticons, slang), specificity/detail level, and readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deceivers may disassociate (non-immediacy), be more informal, or show different specificity/readability profiles. Misspellings are another signal (studied in COVID-19 context). Use style metrics (readability indices, diversity measures) to augment detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic Extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Extract article topics via models like LDA or Markov-inspired topic extraction to represent topical content of headline and body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use topic features individually or combined (headline + body) to enhance classifiers (e.g., combined with BERT). Topic models can detect trends in fake-news agendas over time when applied to fact-checking corpora.

rubrics_metrics.name: User-profile Features
rubrics_metrics.description: Features derived from user profiles and timelines: user description text, posting history, number of friends/followers, timeline content and friend profiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: User-level signals provide context for propagation and credibility. Use profile textual features and network statistics to build richer user representations; these are especially useful when combined with content and propagation features (see Section 6 referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Image-based and Multimodal Features
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual features from embedded images or image-only posts, detection of tampered/out-of-context images, and cross-modal consistency between image and text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply OCR on images with embedded text; use deep learning pipelines for visual-only content. Multimodal models should detect inconsistencies between textual and visual entities. Architectures may include multimodal encoders, text-guided visual generators, image-guided textual decoders, and comment-driven explanation generators; accuracy in cross-modal consistency assessment is challenging but informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: External Evidence / External Feature Integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate external textual information from web search, Wikipedia, and fact-checking services to compute fact-verification or credibility scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approaches include querying search engines using post text, limiting reliable results to popular news sites, and computing similarity (e.g., Levenshtein distance between tweet text and result titles) to yield fact-verification scores. Use references/URLs and fact-checking services (Media Bias/Fact Check) and stance-detection techniques to assess credibility. Be aware of external source reliability and extraction noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propagation Structural Features
rubrics_metrics.description: Network-structure features of propagation/cascade graphs: size (nodes), depth (max root-to-leaf distance), breadth (nodes per level), node centrality (degree, betweenness, closeness), virality (average shortest-path/Wiener index), and modularity/clustering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute features at whole-graph or subgraph levels. Fake vs true news show differences: fake news often spreads faster, broader, deeper (studies show falsehood reached 1,500 people ~6x faster). Use structural metrics as classifier inputs and for behavioral insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propagation Temporal Features
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporal annotations of propagation: lifespan/duration (time between first and last post), speed (time to reach X users or depth), and heat (number of nodes/comments within time interval).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal dynamics differ between fake and true news (falsehood spreads more quickly). Use temporal features for early detection metrics (time-to-threshold) and to capture diffusion velocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propagation Other Features (User & Content Distributions, Cross-network Relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributional features over users involved (e.g., percentage of bots, habitual reaction measures), distribution of content/item features in propagation, and correlations between different networks (e.g., friendship vs retweet likelihood).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include statistics on user behavior, bot involvement, habitual sharing cues (UI affordances), and cross-network correlations. Studies report fake-news cascades being 'more sophisticated' and different across metrics (number of distinct nodes, diameter, Wiener index, structural virality, betweenness, modularity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph-based / Heterogeneous Network Modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Build heterogeneous graphs combining entities (news, posts, users, publishers) and relations (publish, tweet, retweet, follower, citation), apply meta-paths, graph embeddings, GNNs/GATs, graph kernels, and adversarial/topic-discriminator strategies for veracity classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative frameworks: Hetero-SCAN (nodes: publishers/users/news; meta-paths to enrich news node features; KG embeddings like TransE refined for task), SOMPS-Net (social interaction graphs + publisher/news stats fused via graph convolutions and cross-attention), PSIN (post-user interaction networks decomposed into propagation tree, user social graph, and post-user graph; uses GATs and adversarial topic discriminator). Design choices: node types, edge types, initial textual/meta features, choice of graph model and meta-paths; use adversarial components to improve generalizability to new topics.
